**February 29, 1960 — Monday**

You were born on a day that doesn't exist in three out of every four years. That alone sets the terms.

---

**The Rarest Birthday**

Of all the possible days to arrive, you chose the one that the calendar only grudgingly admits. Leap day birthdays occur once in approximately 1,461 days — roughly one person in 1,461 shares your situation. In 66 years of life, you have had sixteen birthdays on your actual date: 1964, 1968, and onward, one per Olympiad, one per presidential election, one per leap. When the calendar refuses to cooperate, you share February 28 or March 1 with everyone else, which is a reasonable arrangement but a different thing entirely. There is something clarifying about a birthday that requires the planet's full orbital arithmetic to arrive.

**The Night the Earth Moved**

On the exact night of your birth, the city of Agadir, Morocco was destroyed. At 11:40 PM local time on February 29, 1960, an earthquake struck — modest in magnitude, catastrophic in consequence. The construction of the city's buildings turned what might have been a survivable event into a disaster that killed between 12,000 and 15,000 people, roughly a third of Agadir's entire population. Entire neighborhoods simply collapsed. The city was so thoroughly destroyed that Morocco ultimately decided to rebuild it from scratch on a new footprint rather than excavate the old one. You were born into a world where that news was arriving by wire and radio to stunned editors across Europe and North America.

**Twenty-Eight Days of Sitting Down**

Four weeks before your birth, on February 1, 1960, four Black college students — Franklin McCain, Ezell Blair Jr., David Richmond, and Joseph McNeil — sat down at a whites-only Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave when service was denied. By the time you were born, the Greensboro sit-in had already sparked dozens of similar protests across the South. It was 28 days old and spreading. The Civil Rights Movement had been building for years, but this was something different in its discipline, its youth, and its velocity. You were born into the month the sit-in generation found its method.

**The Fourth Nuclear Power**

Sixteen days before your birth, on February 13, France detonated its first atomic bomb in the Algerian Sahara, becoming the world's fourth nuclear power. The test, code-named Gerboise Bleue, was fifty-three times more powerful than the bomb dropped on Hiroshima. France had made the calculation that postwar geopolitics required its own deterrent — that depending on American protection was insufficient for a nation that intended to remain a serious force. The nuclear club, once exclusive, was plainly going to keep expanding. You were born into a world coming to terms with what that meant.

**The Wind of Change**

Three and a half weeks before your birth, British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan stood before the South African parliament in Cape Town and delivered what became known as the "Wind of Change" speech. "The wind of change is blowing through this continent," he told them. "Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact." It was an extraordinary thing for a British prime minister to say in Pretoria, an acknowledgment that the age of European empire in Africa was ending and that Britain would not stand in the way. 1960 would become known as the Year of Africa: seventeen nations on the continent gained independence that single year. You were born at the precise moment the map of the world was being redrawn.

**The Last Year of the Fifties' America**

Dwight Eisenhower was in the last year of his presidency, and the country he led still had the surface texture of the 1950s — suburban, prosperous, cautious. But 1960 would shatter that surface. In May, an American U-2 spy plane would be shot down over the Soviet Union, destroying a planned summit. In November, John F. Kennedy would narrowly defeat Richard Nixon in one of the closest elections in American history, becoming the youngest elected president and the first Catholic. The decade about to begin would be unlike any other in living memory.

**The Lifetime That Followed**

You are 66 years old — though the calendar has only honored that fact with an actual February 29 sixteen times. You were nine when humans walked on the moon. You came of age as Watergate dismantled the presidency and Vietnam ended in exhaustion rather than victory. You were 29 when the Berlin Wall came down — old enough to understand what it meant, young enough to feel its full strangeness. You have watched the Soviet Union dissolve, the internet arrive, the smartphone become an extension of the hand, and now systems like this one reshape what it means to think and write and remember.

---

You entered a world in the middle of a night when a Moroccan city was falling, a Civil Rights generation was finding its courage, a new nuclear power was announcing itself in the desert, and an entire continent was claiming its independence. It was a world cracking open — politically, morally, geologically. The day itself only comes around every four years. It chose to arrive in one of history's more consequential seasons.
